text: You're given a list of words, sorted by the rules of an alien language. Recover a possible order of its letters. Return any valid order, or an empty string if the input is contradictory.

Thanks. Before I dive in, I'd like to clarify a few things. Just to make sure I'm understanding this correctly — the words are already sorted by the alien alphabet, and I need to work backward to the letter order. Right? Here's the thing I want to say early. The sort only leaks one clue per neighboring pair. When I compare two words side by side, the first place they differ tells me one letter comes before another. Everything after that first difference tells me nothing. So this is really a graph. Each clue is a directed edge, and I want a topological order of the letters.
That's right. Letters are lowercase a to z.

Let me run through the example: w r t, w r f, e r, e t t, r f t t. Each neighboring pair gives exactly one clue: t before f, w before e, r before t, and e before r. Those edges chain up into w, e, r, t, f — so the order is w e r t f.

Hmm, let me think about this for a sec. A naive approach would be to try every permutation of the letters and check them all. But that's up to twenty-six factorial. Hopeless. This problem reminds me of topological sort. Build a graph of before edges, then flatten it into a line. If the graph has a cycle, the order contradicts itself and I return empty. There are two standard ways to topo-sort, and I'll show both: DFS reverse post-order, and Kahn's BFS on in-degrees.

Here's the plan. I'm using an adjacency set per letter to keep track of the edges. One: add every letter that appears as a node, even with no edges. Two: for each neighboring pair, find the first differing index, add that one edge, and stop. Three: topologically sort the graph, with DFS or Kahn — a cycle means return empty. Two edge cases: the prefix conflict, and lonely letters with no edges. One thing worth flagging. Two words like a b c, then a b, are a contradiction — a prefix must come before the longer word, never after. If I scan the shared length and find no difference but the first word is longer, I return empty right away. Does this approach sound good, or would you rather I think of another way?
Sounds good. Show me both topo sorts.

Alright, let me code this up. First the DFS version, with three colors for cycle detection. Both versions build the graph the same way: register every letter, add one edge per neighboring pair, and return empty on a prefix conflict. One thing worth flagging in the DFS. I add a letter to res only after all its descendants have finished — that's post-order, which is the reverse of topological order, so I flip it at the end. Cycle detection is the gray color: if I reach a node that's still on the recursion stack, I've found a back edge.

Now the same thing with Kahn's BFS. Every letter with in-degree zero starts in the queue; each pop appends the letter and lowers its neighbors' in-degrees. If the result is shorter than the number of letters, something was stuck in a cycle. One thing worth flagging in Kahn's — the count check before the in-degree increment. The same edge can be produced by more than one word pair. The set only stores it once, but if I bump the in-degree every time, the count is too high, that letter never drops to zero, and I'd falsely report a cycle. The DFS version uses a set with no counts, so it's immune.

Let's dry-run the code with the example, through Kahn's. The four edges are t to f, w to e, r to t, and e to r. The row that matters is the start: only w has in-degree zero, so it goes first. Popping it frees e, which frees r, and so on down the chain. The result has five letters, equal to the letter count, so no cycle — w e r t f. Let's also test with corner cases. z, x, z forces z before x and x before z — a cycle, so I return empty. a b c, then a b, is a prefix conflict, empty. A single word like a b c has no pairs, so its letters come out in any order — all valid.

Let me think about complexity here. Time is big O of C plus V plus E, where C is the total length of all words, V is the number of distinct letters, and E is the number of edges. Building the graph scans every character once; the topo sort touches each node and edge once. Both versions are the same. Space is big O of V plus E, for the graph plus the color map or the in-degree map. In the worst case V is capped at twenty-six, so the letter part is basically constant. Oh, one more thing — if I needed the smallest valid order instead of any, I'd take the Kahn version and swap the plain queue for a min-heap, always popping the smallest ready letter. The DFS version doesn't give that as cleanly.

Nice. Three things stood out. You saw early that only the first differing character carries order info, and you caught the prefix-conflict edge case. You showed both topo skeletons, DFS reverse post-order and Kahn. And you flagged the dedup trap in Kahn's in-degree — a real bug that a set-based DFS avoids for free. Strong hire.
